<pre>
--- Log opened Tue Mar 11 00:00:29 2003
00:12 -!- jal0 [~not@12-243-94-89.client.attbi.com] has quit []
08:40  * mouse is back (gone 17:37:31)
09:30  * mouse is away: gotta work
10:23 -!- jal0 [~not@12-243-94-89.client.attbi.com] has joined #linux4be
10:27 < mouse> jal0 hi
10:27 < jal0> hey mouse
10:27 < jal0> how's it going
10:30 < mouse> jal0 I have a lot of work ;-(( at end of march, I'll return to develop touchpanel...
10:31 < jal0> ok
10:32 < jal0> i feel your pain :)
10:36 < mouse> ;-)
11:00 -!- andrey [~andrey@66.33.46.16] has joined #linux4be
11:00 < andrey> hi guys!
11:05 < mouse> andrey: hi
11:06 < andrey> how is it going?
11:06 < andrey> Still a lot of work?
11:07 < mouse> aga
11:07 < andrey> :-)
11:09 < andrey> Do you know how interrupts are processed? I was trying to look into it. I'm curiuos whether I can change GIU interrupt processing.
11:09 < jal0> hey andrey
11:10 < jal0> how interrupts are processed... in linux or CE?
11:11 < andrey> hi jal0
11:11 < andrey> in linux. I see that there are 32 interrupts reserved for GIU. And this number is hardcoded in at least two files.
11:12 < jal0> yeap, but you can have more by chaining them
11:12 < andrey> But in BE there are more than 32. Unless one irq is assigned to all cascading interrupts...
11:13 < andrey> but how to distinguish them?
11:14 < jal0> normally it's done by asking each prepherial device "was it you".
11:15 < jal0> this asking is done in priority manner
11:15 < jal0> where high devices get asked first
11:16 < andrey> ic. 
11:18 < jal0> normally the device has more than one interrupt source, so once it is know that that device was the source of the intterupt, a more percise handler is called which uses registers on the external device to determine the exact nature of the interrupt
11:19 < andrey> I just noticed giu_cascade irqaction in the source code and I thought it's irqs 40-71 for first level and maybe 72-whatever for second, etc...
11:20 < jal0> not sure what you mean... where in the sources are you looking
11:20 < andrey> linux kernel
11:21 < andrey> ok, maybe I need to understand it better :-)
11:22 < jal0> there was  a real good link on the web, that explained how irq's work in linux. i'll try to find it again, as it was lost when my harddrive crashed. I really suck at trying to explain things :(
11:23 < jal0> btw, did you get my standalone dissembler to compile
11:23 < andrey> I mean for BE-200 GIU_IRQ_0 is cascading. Does it mean that all second level interrupts have the same IRQ number?
11:23 < andrey> Yes, I compiled it today. And it works! :-)
11:23 < jal0> i think so
11:25 < andrey> Don't worry, it's not you (about explaining things) I always jump into conclusions instead of thinking little bit more :-)
11:25 < jal0> each GUI_IRQ_XX is for an external device, the external device may have more that one interrupt source. example is a uart, most signal interrupts when data has been received and when tx-buffer is empty and several others. but the external uart only has on irq line that goes back to the cpu
11:26 < jal0> has on irq = has one irg
11:26 < jal0> irg= irq
11:26 < jal0> ugg... :)
11:27 < jal0> so the uart has a status register which you can look at to determine the exact interrupt that was signaled
11:28 < jal0> have you got a uart datasheet around?
11:28 < andrey> I mean not several interrupts for the same device, but several devices on the same interrupt
11:29 < andrey> no, I don't. why?
11:30 < jal0> its the same principle, except the external device it an irq controller
11:33 < jal0> say GUI_IRQ_01 is attached to an irq controller, that controller has 8 input sources which eight external devices are attached to. if any of those devices cause an interrupt, the GUI_IRQ_01 is signalled. in the handler routine, the cpu reads the status register of the irq handler to determine which device signalled the interrupt. then another handler reads the registers on the external device to determine the exact source
11:33 < jal0> and so one for the depth of the chain
11:34 < jal0> and so one= and so on
11:35 < andrey> You mean that if touch panel and buttons share the same primary interrupt both controller should know how to read status register and determine whether it's their device?
11:37 < jal0> yes, it means that there is a status register somewhere that will tell you wich device actually caused the interrupt. then the device itself has a register that will tell you what the exact cause of the interrupt on the device was
11:38 < andrey> ic.
11:39 < jal0> if two devices share the same interrupt, then its two levels of registers you have to read in order to determine the exact cause of the interrupt
11:40 < jal0> another good source of general info on irq handling would be any tutorial on the pc, the hardware is the same, onle the code is different
11:40 < jal0> but to understand the code, you really have to understand the hardware first
11:40 < andrey> I understand that. I was just wondering who reads these registers. Is it common interrupts processing code or each device driver reads it again in its turn.
11:42 < andrey> When I started to learn PC there was no such thing as "interrupt sharing", it was "interrupt conflict" :-))
11:42 < jal0> usually there is a common irq handler for each level of irq casqading which is used to determine the actual device, then a specific handler for each device
11:42 < jal0> :)
11:44 < andrey> Than this common handler should either know which driver is interested in which bit (or value) in status register ot should generate another interrupt signal that driver should subscribe to
11:44 < andrey> Than = then (?)
11:44 < jal0> the commone irq handlers are managed by the OS, where as the specific handler is part of the device driver and registers with the OS so it 'know how to find it'
11:45 < jal0> hmm, say that again
11:45 < jal0> only one interrupt is ever generated
11:45 < andrey> Again, suppose we have irq0 that is shared between touch screen and keyboard.
11:46 < andrey> There is common handler that knows how to read some status register to distinguish it.
11:47 < andrey> What does this handler do after that? Does it call either touch driver or keyboard driver based on status register value?
11:47 < jal0> yes, and in that case there is an external controller that holds the register for this 
11:48 < jal0> the keyboard and touchscreen are inputs to this controller and are not connected to the cpu. when irq0 is signalled, the cpu reads the status register on the irq controller which usually is a bit mask of the devices it receives input from.
11:49 < jal0> this determines what device actually signalled the interrupt
11:49 < jal0> then the device driver for that  device is called to handle it
11:51 < andrey> So if I write touch panel driver I should not only register for irq0 (or even not to register at all) but also tell this controller that my bit in status register is 0? Or is it kind of hardcoded in this controller?
11:51 < jal0> usually the device driver reads registers from the device to determine the exact cause of the irq because the device can have more than one source of interrupt. but the irq controller only know 'something' happend, not exactly what
11:52 < andrey> Ok, I think I'm lost. Probably it's better to read something about it than ask you to explain obvious things.
11:52 < jal0> it's hardwired in the controller, unless of course we have a programmable irq controller. but untill we have all the interrupts mapped out, it would probably be best to use the mappings set by the CE
11:53 < jal0> so in effect, treat is as being hardwired
11:55 < andrey> Ok, let's talk about real life than. :-) In BE-300 GIU_IRQ_0 is shared. You need to read [AA000004]. If bit 0 is set then it's PCMCIA.
11:55 < jal0> the problem is not in creating the drivers for the touchpanel, it's in creating the driver for the controller. unless you know all the devices that attach to it, it's going to be hard to write any code that dosn't break linux during boot.
11:55 < jal0> ok
11:56 < andrey> If it's 1 then it's buttons and if it's bit 9 it's touch panel.
11:56 < jal0> so thats the register in the controller
11:57 < andrey> Where in the kernel code should I put this knowledge - in some commone code or in each device driver?
11:57 < jal0> in a common irq handler
11:58 < andrey> Ok. How this common handler knows that if bit 1 is set it should call keyboard driver?
11:58 < jal0> the irq handler should not have to know anything about WHAT is causing the interrupt, only WHO to call when it does
11:58 < jal0> the keyboard driver should register with it during boot
11:59 < andrey> And tell the controller that "I'm interesting in bit 1"?
11:59 < jal0> keep and array of functions that reperesent the bit locations in the controller register
12:00 < jal0> the driver puts it's init function there when registering.
12:00 < andrey> So controller will call all three driver in hope of one of them "accepts" the interrupt?
12:00 < jal0> yeap
12:01 < andrey> Ok, now I understand. I hope... :-)
12:02 < jal0> the function should only read another register on the device to see if it was the source of the interrupt, if not it moves to the next one down the line, as so on until all devices have been asked
12:02 < jal0> this array is also set up so high priority interrupts sources get looked at first
12:03 < andrey> But then I don't understand what's the purpose of defining GIUINT_CASCADE_IRQ in linux code. Because it assumes special processing for this particular IRQ.
12:03 < jal0> i'm not sure, i'd have to look at the code
12:04 < andrey> Well, it's little bit messy. :-) There are functions that are never called. Al least I didn't find... :-)
12:07 < jal0> what i was talking about above you should mostly not have to do, the common code is already written. This is where the real problem is. If you enable the irq handling mechinism in the linux kernel, then you have to have in place handlers for the core devices, otherwise, the kernel will not boot
12:08 < jal0> right now, most of the irq handling is done from code, setup from CE
12:09 < jal0> once you hook in the linux irq handling code, that code goes away. stuff like handling the watchdog, timers, etc. is handled though code setup from CE
12:12 < andrey> But for now (if I understand it right) we just need to register touch panel driver for giu_irq_0 and add to this driver some code for reading and analyzing register AA000004
12:15 < jal0> i recommend this, find where in CE the drivers are registered, then overwrite this 'slot' with your own handler function pointer
12:16 < jal0> i don't think you can fully enable irq handling in linux without setting up core system irq's
12:17 < jal0> hence the 2-minute reset issue we had a while back
12:18 < andrey> Why are you laking about CE? linux kernel has it's own interrupt handling, doesn't it?
12:18 < jal0> yes, but its not 'Really' being used
12:18 < jal0> unless, things have changed since the last time i looked at the code
12:19 < andrey> We use CE initialization code but after the kernel is loaded I doubt that CE "sees" a single interrupt.
12:19 < jal0> which was a while ago, so maybe i should revisit it
12:20 < jal0> the irq vector table is a hardcoded memory location that the cpu jumps to when it recieves an interrupt
12:20 < jal0> its not software controlled
12:20 < jal0> so unless you overwrite this jump to address, the cpu WILL try and execute code located there
12:21 < jal0> the last i looked, this 'jump-to' address was still populated with CE default code
12:21 < jal0> the OS does NOT see irq's, it the cpu
12:22 < jal0> hmm, did that make any sense ?-)
12:23 < jal0> let me grab my data books and i'll give you a reference to looks at
12:24 < andrey> But all CPU does is jump to 80000180. And this handler is populated with the except_vec3_r4000 handler (see arch/mips/kernel/traps.c)
12:27 < jal0> hmm, looking for 80000180 in the data books... remember the page?
12:27 < andrey> What book?
12:28 < jal0> vr series manual
12:28 < andrey> Vr4131 user's manual, page 86
12:29 < andrey> vr series architecture, page 75
12:31 < jal0> ok, indeed. NMI's have seperate vector
12:31 < jal0> so irq handling for device should indeed be possible
12:33 < jal0> " register touch panel driver for giu_irq_0 and add to this driver some code for reading and analyzing register AA000004 " <--- yes
12:34 < andrey> It's good that we don't need to change existing code. :-)
12:34 < jal0> sorry, i work with different micro's at my job, and sometime confuse them :)
12:35 < jal0> i tried a while back to get rid of the '2-minute' reset problem by overwriting the NMI code, i couldn't get it to work and everything seemed to break
12:37 < jal0> ok, time for me to go to work now. so i know, you are going to be working on the touch panel code?
12:38 < andrey> ic. btw while looking into iterrupt processing I noticed several registers CE put some values into on each timer tick. Maybe it can resolve th reboot issue.
12:39 < andrey> I was thinking about it but I'm afraid mouse will have time for it earlier than I understand how linux drivers work :-)
12:39 < jal0> it's something to look into, but now that i'm using expod, that issue seemed to go away so i havn't look into it any further
12:40 < andrey> Maybe we'll return to if when (if) we decide to bypass CE initialization code.
12:40 < jal0> i know what you mean, this is my first go at linux kernel hack also. 
12:40 < andrey> :-)
12:41 < jal0> but for the most part, the hardest thing is being able to follow the code. i've be using redhat's 'Sourcer' code browser and it has helped alot.
12:42 < jal0> ok, anyway talk to you later
12:43 -!- jal0 is now known as jal0_wrkn
12:43 < mouse> andrey: =)
12:45 < andrey> jal0 later
